memory_candidates.content: A bash/PCRE checker using a trailing `\b` word-boundary to confirm a declaration name's end will silently conflate a primed identifier (`foo'`) with its unprimed counterpart (`foo`), in both directions: an unprimed search can be falsely satisfied by a primed declaration (since word-char -> prime is itself a `\b` transition), and a primed search can fail to match its own primed declaration if followed by whitespace (prime -> whitespace is non-word -> non-word, no transition, `\b` never fires). Fix: replace the trailing `\b` with a negative lookahead for every character that can continue the identifier, e.g. `(?![A-Za-z0-9_'])`, which states directly what is meant instead of relying on a word/non-word transition that primes break.

When a grep-based Lean declaration-existence checker searches for `keyword\s+bare_name\b`, it misses the common Lean 4 style of writing a dot-qualified declaration name directly after the keyword with no surrounding `namespace ... end` block (e.g. `def TaskFrame.ValidOn (...) := ...`). If a namespace/end-line fallback in the same checker already allows an optional `(\S+\.)?` prefix, the main keyword branch almost certainly needs the identical prefix -- an asymmetry between the two branches is a strong signal of an unintentional gap, not a deliberate design choice.

Before triaging a mechanical checker's findings into per-finding decisions, re-verify the checker itself is correct -- a finding list built against a buggy checker produces a ledger full of false positives that must be re-discovered and corrected later. Fixing checker bugs mid-triage (even if nominally a later phase's territory) and re-running before classifying is more efficient than classifying stale output and re-triaging after the fix.
